name: Syringobulbia
system: Nervous system / Spinal cord and brainstem

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A fluid-filled cavity within the brainstem, usually the medulla, most often representing rostral extension of a cervical syringomyelia along the tegmentum rather than an isolated lesion

Involvement of the lower cranial nerve nuclei produces dysphagia, dysarthria, palatal and pharyngeal weakness, and tongue wasting with fasciculation, so the picture can superficially resemble a bulbar motor syndrome
Damage to the descending spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve gives a dissociated facial sensory loss in an onion-skin or balaclava distribution, a highly suggestive sign
Nystagmus, particularly downbeat, together with vertigo and oscillopsia reflects involvement of vestibular connections and the medial longitudinal fasciculus
An ipsilateral Horner syndrome may occur from interruption of descending sympathetic fibres in the brainstem
The disorder is strongly associated with Chiari I malformation and obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow at the foramen magnum, and less often with trauma or intramedullary tumour
MRI of the brain and whole spine is the investigation of choice and typically shows the brainstem cavity in continuity with a cervical cord syrinx
Progressive bulbar involvement threatens the airway through aspiration, vocal cord palsy and central respiratory disturbance, so surveillance of swallowing and breathing is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Syringobulbia is a slit-like, gliosis-lined cavity within the brainstem, most commonly dissecting through the medullary tegmentum, and in the majority of cases it is continuous with a cervical cord syrinx. It is thought to arise from disordered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics at the craniovertebral junction, classically in association with a Chiari I malformation, which alters pressure gradients and drives fluid into and along the neuraxis. As the cavity enlarges it disrupts adjacent structures, including the nuclei and intramedullary fibres of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and hypoglossal nerves, the spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, descending sympathetic pathways, the medial longitudinal fasciculus and vestibular connections, producing the characteristic constellation of bulbar, sensory, oculomotor and autonomic signs.
additionalDifferentials: Brainstem glioma or other intrinsic brainstem tumour
Foramen magnum or craniovertebral junction tumour
Brainstem cavernoma or other vascular malformation
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and whole spine with contrast to define the brainstem cavity and any continuous cord syrinx
Cine phase-contrast (CSF flow) MRI at the craniovertebral junction to assess for obstruction and a Chiari I malformation
Dedicated imaging of the craniovertebral junction and skull base to identify structural causes
Videofluoroscopic or fibreoptic swallowing assessment to quantify aspiration risk
Laryngoscopy to evaluate vocal cord and palatal function
Overnight oximetry or polysomnography where central sleep-disordered breathing is suspected
redFlags: Progressive bulbar dysfunction with clinical or objective evidence of aspiration
Stridor or vocal cord paralysis, or symptoms of central sleep apnoea suggesting respiratory compromise
Rapid neurological deterioration indicating cavity expansion
New or worsening brainstem signs in a patient with known syringomyelia
reference.prognosis: The course is usually slowly progressive over years, and treatment directed at the underlying cause, such as posterior fossa decompression for Chiari I malformation, may arrest or partially reverse deficits. Established bulbar and cranial nerve deficits often persist, and advanced disease carries a risk of life-threatening aspiration and respiratory compromise.
pitfalls: Attributing tongue wasting and bulbar weakness to motor neurone disease without imaging the brainstem and cervical cord
Failing to recognise the onion-skin facial sensory loss as a localising trigeminal tract sign
Overlooking an associated Chiari I malformation or craniovertebral junction abnormality that is amenable to treatment
Not imaging the whole neuraxis and thereby missing a continuous cervical syrinx
Underestimating occult central sleep-disordered breathing and aspiration risk
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
